title: Time-Restricted Eating Linked to Improved Huntington’s Disease Markers
content:
The first clinical study to understand the potential effects of time-restricted eating in people with Huntington’s disease finds that time-restricted eating is feasible, safe, and linked to improvements in disease markers.
In a 12-week pilot study, researchers found that people with early-stage Huntington’s Disease were able to safely follow a form of intermittent fasting known as time-restricted eating—limiting food consumption to a six-to-eight-hour window each day. Participants avoided unintended weight loss and showed improvements in measures of disease severity; in a blood biomarker linked to nerve cell damage; and in cellular energy production.
The findings are published today in Nature Metabolism, in the paper “Effects of time-restricted eating in early-stage Huntington’s disease: a pilot study.”
“This is the first time this approach has been formally studied in people with Huntington’s disease,” said Russell Wells, a medical student at Oregon Health & Science University. “We found that participants were able to follow the eating schedule, maintain their weight and show encouraging improvements in clinical and biological measures that are important in Huntington’s disease. These results suggest time-restricted eating deserves further study in a larger clinical trial.”
Huntington’s disease is a rare, inherited neurological disease that gradually damages nerve cells responsible for movement, cognitive and emotional regulation. Although researchers have known the genetic cause of the disease for decades, no treatments have been approved that slow or stop its progression.
Prior research in animal models suggests that intermittent fasting can activate cellular pathways that help protect brain cells. Yet researchers were unsure whether the approach would be safe for people with Huntington’s disease because unintended weight loss is already a concern.
“When Russell first brought me the idea, I was skeptical,” notes Amie Hiller, MD, professor of neurology in the OHSU School of Medicine and director of the Portland Veteran’s Administration Northwest Parkinson’s Disease Research, Education and Clinical Center. “Weight loss is a major challenge for many people with Huntington’s disease, so asking them to eat within a limited time window seemed counterintuitive.
“What was exciting about this study is that participants were able to maintain their weight while showing signs that the intervention may be positively affecting the disease itself,” Hiller notes.
The 20 participants selected an eating window that fit their daily routine, typically between late morning and early evening, and followed it for 12 weeks. Researchers encouraged participants to maintain their normal calorie intake and monitored weight and safety throughout the study.
The approach appeared well-tolerated. Participants followed the eating schedule on average more than five days per week; reported few side effects; and maintained both body weight and lean muscle mass. Most adapted to the schedule within the first one to two weeks. Participants used a smartphone app to document their first meal of the day with a photo and timestamp.
Participants experienced an average improvement of 0.5 points on a widely used Huntington’s disease severity scale known as the composite Unified Huntington’s Disease Rating Scale (cUHDRS). The score typically declines by about one point annually in people with early-stage disease.
In addition, blood levels of neurofilament light, a biomarker released when nerve cells are damaged, fell by an average of 13%. In Huntington’s disease, those levels usually increase over time as the disease progresses.
“We saw a reversal of the trend we would normally expect,” Wells said. “Neurofilament light typically rises as neurodegeneration continues, but after three months we observed a significant decrease. For a pilot study, that was a remarkable finding.”
The research team also examined mitochondrial function in participants’ blood cells and found improvements in several measures of mitochondrial activity after the intervention.
“One theory is that fasting acts as a mild stressor that prompts cells to become more efficient,” Wells said. “If cells, including brain cells, become better at producing energy and handling stress, they may be more resilient to the disease process.”
Because the study was small and did not include a comparison group, researchers caution that the findings should not be considered proof that time-restricted eating slows Huntington’s disease. Larger, randomized controlled trials will be needed to determine whether the benefits are real and sustained over time.
Still, researchers say the results are especially promising because the intervention is relatively simple and could be accessible to many people as there are no disease-modifying treatments for Huntington’s disease currently available. The team is currently pursuing funding for a larger, randomized clinical trial that would compare time-restricted eating with standard dietary habits.

title: Tchad : solidarité à l'Ennedi-Ouest, les anciens élèves redonnent vie à l'École pilote de Kalaït
content:
Tchad : solidarité à l'Ennedi-Ouest, les anciens élèves redonnent vie à l'École pilote de Kalaït
Dans la province de l'Ennedi-Ouest, les anciens élèves de l'École pilote de Kalaït ont achevé la deuxième phase des travaux de réfection de leur établissement d'origine.
Les anciens élèves de l'École pilote de Kalaït ont récemment achevé la deuxième phase des travaux de réfection de leur ancien établissement, situé dans la province de l'Ennedi-Ouest.
Ils ont consacré leur temps à la réfection des bâtiments, notamment au remplacement des planches usées et des toitures. Les travaux de clôture ont par ailleurs été complétés par la plantation d'arbustes dans la cour de l'école.
« Nous sommes redevables envers cette école historique qui nous a tant donné et qui a formé de nombreux cadres de ce pays, dans différents domaines, ainsi que des personnes influentes », a indiqué l'un des initiateurs, Abdramane Koré Djouma.
Après des années de dégradation, cette école retrouve aujourd'hui son éclat d'antan. Son image rayonne à nouveau.
Cette initiative a pu se matérialiser grâce à l'apport des anciens ressortissants et aux diverses contributions modestes des uns et des autres.
« Aujourd'hui, nous avons payé ensemble une partie de notre dette morale envers cette école. Et nous continuerons à la payer encore et encore, jusqu'à ce que notre école retrouve pleinement son souffle d'antan », a martelé Abdramane Koré Djouma.

title: Unfinished peace process: What’s next after BARMM polls?
content:
Unfinished peace process: What’s next after BARMM polls?
MANILA, Philippines — After Monday’s parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), a key achievement for the peace process, civil society advocates are now calling attention to the need to complete the normalization effort for former Moro combatants and their war-torn communities before the country is caught in the frenzy of the 2028 elections.
In the wee hours of Wednesday, the regional board of canvassers led by Bangsamoro Election Director Ray Sumalipao confirmed the selection of two representatives who will take the parliament seats reserved for non-Moro indigenous peoples.
After that came the most awaited proclamation of the victory of four regional parliamentary political parties and the corresponding nominees who will take 40 of 80 seats in the first elected regional legislature.
As the last party nominee was proclaimed, the historic political exercise came to a close, completing the political track laid out in the landmark Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB) that aims to usher former rebel forces from armed struggle to democratic self-governance.
Signed in 2014 between the government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), the CAB puts an end to over four decades of secessionist rebellion in Mindanao.
READ: Parties led by ex-rebels dominate BARMM polls
The Bangsamoro Organic Law (BOL), the major instrument to implement the CAB, sought to bring in the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), the original secessionist movement, into the BARMM’s embrace. This was achieved with key MNLF factions joining the interim regional government, and eventually building political parties that vied for seats in Monday’s elections.
Big step, new blood
Political scientist Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, a former government chief negotiator with the MILF, emphasized that the parliamentary system in the BARMM managed to draw the participation of the MNLF, which also signed a peace pact with the government in 1996.
“It’s the first time the MNLF formed a political party (and joined the parliamentary elections). They never did that before,” she said during a roundtable discussion with Inquirer editors and reporters on Tuesday, the day after the BARMM elections.
The MNLF factions of Nur Misuari and Muslimin Sema joined the parliamentary race through the Mahardika Party and Bangsamoro Party, respectively. “That’s a big step—that we have former armed groups that are really serious about party building now, precisely because of the parliamentary system,” Coronel-Ferrer said.
Former Presidential Peace Adviser Teresita Quintos Deles noted that the parliamentary system also managed to somehow made a dent on the entrenched dominance of political dynasties in the region.
This was shown in the impressive showing of the MILF’s United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) in the region-wide vote, capturing all six sectoral seats and taking 15 of 40 seats for party representation.
The UBJP also captured nine parliamentary district seats, with big wins in three of nine constituencies in Lanao del Sur province where its candidates faced the political might of dynastic clans.
“We see (the entry of) new blood and we are very hopeful. Because of the party system, you have a lot of new people and young people who got their names listed,” Deles said. “They entered politics carrying parties with platforms and positions on issues. It was certainly refreshing for us considering what we’re seeing,” she added.
These achievements outweighed the grim incidents that attended the poll conduct, especially the death of four people in election-related violence, and allegations of vote-buying and ballot padding, said Kiko Aquino Dee, who joins Deles and Coronel-Ferrer as co-convenors of the multisectoral coalition Duyog Bangsamoro.
Presidential Peace Adviser Mel Senen Sarmiento said it was saddening that violence still attended to the historic exercise, although it was a consolation the level and degree were nothing compared to previous ones.
On Wednesday, Commission on Elections Chair George Erwin Garcia said that on Election Day “the sound of restraint was louder than the rumblings of trouble” which contributed to the 84.43-percent voter turnout—unprecedented in the region’s history.
Still a lot ahead
As the incoming members of parliament organize themselves into the regional government by Oct. 30, Deles cautions against resting on these recent laurels.
She said having the parliamentary elections was not the conclusion of the CAB implementation since the accord also encompasses the normalization track.
This includes the decommissioning of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front’s (MILF) combat forces and their weapons, the transformation of MILF camps, the redeployment of government troops, the disbandment of private armies, and the pursuit of transitional justice and reconciliation, among others.
In July last year, the MILF suspended the final phase of the decommissioning process, involving close to 14,000 combatants and 2,450 weapons, until the government could substantially comply with the socioeconomic package for deactivated fighters as agreed by the parties. This was after President Marcos appointed Abdulraof Macacua as interim chief minister in March that year, replacing MILF chief Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim.
So far, a total of 26,145 MILF combatants had been decommissioned, or 65 percent of the 40,000-strong Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces. Deles noted that the initiatives under the socioeconomic aspect was way behind the political track.
Also falling behind in pace is the establishment of a transitional justice and reconciliation (TJR) process that seeks to right historical wrongs against the Bangsamoro people and embark on efforts at social healing to address individual and collective trauma due to the decades-long conflict.
Deles notes that while a TJR program is being shaped in the BARMM, there needs to be a national one, and such effort has yet to start through legislation.
This is why there is a need to keep national interest on and set an “irreversible momentum” for the Bangsamoro peace process.
While Coronel-Ferrer notes about the durability of the CAB compared to other peace pacts forged in other parts of the world in recent times, Deles is worried this might get caught up again by the shaping dynamics of the political transition in 2028 when the country goes into a presidential election.
Deles recalled that at the start of the Duterte presidency, it still took time to muster the BOL even as his party had dominant numbers in Congress.
Prior to Monday’s elections, Duyog Bangsamoro facilitated the signing of a covenant of commitment toward peaceful elections as well as unstinting support to the full implementation of the CAB, especially the normalization track, that should lead to the eventual conclusion of an exit agreement between the government and the MILF.
Huge potentials
The MILF, according to Deles, also recognized the need to complete the decommissioning of its former combatant forces, whatever happens in the vote.
“The potential of economic development in the area is so huge. A peaceful BARMM is good not just for BARMM business; it’s good for the national business sector,” Deles said.
Coronel-Ferrer echoed Deles’ sentiments, citing the importance of sustaining the gains ushered in by the Bangsamoro peace process, including the conduct of the first parliamentary elections in the region. “The development potentials [of the region] are really big. So sayang kung mawaldas ’yung momentum,” she said.
Since the signing of the CAB 12 years ago, the Bangsamoro region has been relatively peaceful, gradually attracting investments, including from foreigners. Last year, the region registered P5.1 billion in investments, beating its annual target of P3 billion. /cb /atm

title: Côte d’Ivoire-AIP/ Rentrée scolaire : Face au regard des autres, le parcours du combattant des enfants en situation de handicap (Reportage)
content:
Abidjan, lundi 21 sept 2026 (AIP) – Derrière les cartables neufs et l’enthousiasme de la rentrée des classes, les enfants vulnérables et en situation de handicap abordent la nouvelle année scolaire avec une préoccupation cruciale : trouver leur place. Entre l’urgence de structures adaptées et le besoin vital d’un regard bienveillant, retour sur ces établissements d’Abidjan où l’inclusion scolaire se bâtit au quotidien, à force de courage et d’adaptation.
Du préscolaire du CAFOP d’Anyama-Ahouabo aux salles de classe de l’ONG REMAR, les initiatives locales se multiplient pour briser les barrières de la différence. Sensibilisation des élèves, aménagements de rampes d’accès ou recherche autonome de méthodes pédagogiques palliatives : les enseignants redoublent d’efforts malgré le manque de moyens didactiques.
Un combat quotidien résumé par le témoignage poignant de mères et d’éducateurs déterminés à faire en sorte que chaque enfant, quelle que soit sa vulnérabilité, puisse apprendre, jouer et grandir sans honte ni isolement.
Apprendre sans honte : le combat d’une fillette et de sa mère pour l’intégration
Une réalité que connaît bien une fillette de bientôt neuf ans, dont le parcours témoigne des difficultés qui peuvent accompagner un enfant en situation de handicap jusque dans la cour de l’école.
Son handicap est apparu alors qu’elle n’avait que six mois. L’une de ses jambes étant plus courte que l’autre, elle doit porter un appareil ainsi qu’une chaussure adaptée pour faciliter ses déplacements.
Mais si cet équipement l’aide à marcher, il ne suffit pas toujours à lui rendre le quotidien scolaire plus facile.
Le regard des autres enfants peut également devenir une source de souffrance. Lorsqu’elle se sent observée avec insistance par ses camarades, la fillette peut se mettre à pleurer.
Pour sa maman, Mlle Adouko Cha Marie Stéphania, il faut alors l’aider à comprendre sa différence, mais aussi à ne pas en avoir honte.
À chaque changement d’établissement, la maman prend le temps d’expliquer la situation aux enseignants et aux élèves afin de faciliter l’intégration de sa fille et d’éviter que le handicap ne devienne un motif d’isolement.
« On la présente dans toutes les classes pour dire que c’est votre camarade, mais elle a un souci […] donc on joue avec elle, elle fait doucement », témoigne Mlle Adouko Cha Marie Stéphania.
Derrière cette démarche, un souhait simple : que sa fille puisse être considérée comme une élève parmi les autres, avec la possibilité d’apprendre, de jouer et de participer pleinement à la vie de l’école.
Au-delà des murs : Quand l’inclusion repose sur l’engagement des enseignants
« Quand un parent vient, je demande tout ce qu’il faut au niveau de l’enfant […] de telle sorte qu’on sache à quel enfant on a affaire et, si on peut au sein de notre établissement aider, on le fait », explique Mme Bini Viviane Pélagie, directrice du préscolaire et tenante de la grande section à l’École d’application du CAFOP d’Abidjan, à Anyama-Ahouabo,
Dans l’établissement, quelques aménagements permettent également de faciliter les déplacements de certains élèves. Un accès permet notamment à un enfant en fauteuil roulant de rejoindre sa classe.
Mais l’inclusion ne se joue pas uniquement dans l’aménagement des bâtiments. Elle se construit aussi dans la cour, dans les salles de classe et dans le regard porté par les autres enfants.
Mme Bini Viviane Pélagie explique que des discussions, des lectures et des histoires permettent d’aborder avec les enfants la question du handicap et de leur apprendre à considérer leurs camarades au-delà de leur différence.
« Parce que ce n’est pas parce qu’il a quelque chose en moins que c’est un enfant qui n’a pas sa place ici. Il a sa place aussi parce que lui aussi c’est un être humain », insiste-t-elle.
Mais intégrer un enfant ayant des besoins particuliers demande aussi davantage d’attention de la part des enseignants.
Dans une classe où une seule enseignante doit déjà accompagner plusieurs élèves, consacrer du temps supplémentaire à un enfant en situation de handicap peut représenter une difficulté.
« Nous avons plusieurs enfants, mais spécialement il faut s’occuper d’eux », souligne Mme Bini Viviane Pélagie.
L’accompagnement suppose alors de mieux observer l’enfant, de comprendre ses besoins et, lorsque cela est possible, d’adapter les méthodes utilisées en classe.
À cette difficulté s’ajoute le manque de matériel pédagogique adapté. Pour y faire face, Mme Bini Viviane Pélagie explique rechercher elle-même des informations et ajuster ses méthodes en fonction des enfants accueillis.
Dans cet établissement, l’inclusion repose ainsi en partie sur les capacités d’adaptation de l’équipe éducative et sur le dialogue avec les familles.
Au-delà du handicap : Quand l’ONG REMAR prend le relais de la vulnérabilité sociale
Mais à quelques kilomètres de là, une autre réalité rappelle que la vulnérabilité scolaire ne concerne pas uniquement le handicap.
Au complexe scolaire REMAR, la rentrée a également commencé. Dans cet établissement, qui peut accueillir environ 300 élèves, deux catégories d’enfants se côtoient : ceux qui viennent à l’école dans le cadre habituel de leur scolarité et ceux qui sont directement pris en charge par l’ONG REMAR.
Ici, l’école fait partie d’un dispositif plus large. « Il y a des enfants de REMAR qui sont là. Comme l’école appartient à la structure ONG REMAR, c’est l’ONG qui s’occupe d’eux », explique Kacou Kofi Bertin, directeur des études du complexe scolaire REMAR.
Au moment du reportage, les inscriptions viennent à peine de commencer. Il est donc encore difficile d’établir le nombre exact d’enfants directement pris en charge par l’organisation. « On vient de commencer, on ne peut pas avoir totalement le nombre des enfants qui sont à la charge », précise le directeur des études.
Pour ces enfants, la scolarité s’inscrit ainsi dans une prise en charge qui dépasse le cadre de la salle de classe. L’ONG doit également mobiliser les ressources nécessaires au fonctionnement de l’établissement et à la prise en charge des enfants concernés.
Selon le directeur des études, cette mobilisation permet notamment de couvrir les dépenses liées au fonctionnement de l’école. « Même pour payer nos salaires, ils pourvoient encore. L’ONG trouve les ressources nécessaires pour y faire face », affirme-t-il.
Si la prise en charge existe, les besoins matériels ne disparaissent pas pour autant. Dans les salles de classe, le matériel pédagogique disponible ne permet pas de répondre à tous les besoins de l’établissement.
« Au niveau du matériel, nous n’avons pas totalement tout ce dont nous avons besoin. Mais ce qui est là peut nous permettre de fonctionner », reconnaît Kacou Kofi Bertin.
En cette journée de rentrée, les équipes éducatives reprennent donc leurs activités avec les moyens disponibles, tandis que les élèves prennent progressivement leurs marques.
D’un établissement à l’autre, les situations diffèrent. À Anyama-Ahouabo, l’enjeu est notamment de permettre aux enfants en situation de handicap de prendre part à la vie scolaire sans être mis à l’écart. À REMAR, il s’agit aussi d’assurer la continuité scolaire d’enfants pris en charge par une organisation qui doit mobiliser les ressources nécessaires à leur accompagnement.
Bien plus qu’un cartable : Trouver sa place dans l’école de demain
Pour certains élèves, cette rentrée commence avec un cartable neuf, des cahiers et l’impatience de retrouver les camarades.
Pour d’autres, elle commence par des préoccupations supplémentaires : un équipement médical à prévoir, un accompagnement particulier à organiser, des enseignants à informer ou encore un regard à apprivoiser.
Le défi est alors de faire de l’école un espace où la différence ne devient pas un obstacle à la scolarisation.
Car derrière chaque inscription, il y a un enfant qui doit pouvoir apprendre, jouer, se faire des amis et grandir avec les autres.
À l’École d’application du CAFOP d’Abidjan, à Anyama-Ahouabo, comme au complexe scolaire REMAR, cette rentrée montre ainsi que pour les enfants les plus vulnérables, le chemin de l’école ne commence pas toujours avec la première sonnerie.
Il commence parfois bien avant, avec une famille qui cherche des solutions, un enseignant qui adapte sa manière de faire, une structure qui mobilise des ressources et une communauté scolaire qui apprend à regarder autrement.
Pour ces enfants, avoir une place à l’école, c’est finalement bien plus que pouvoir s’asseoir dans une salle de classe. C’est pouvoir y apprendre, y évoluer avec les autres et envisager, comme tous les élèves, la suite de son parcours.
Reportage réalisé par Andréa Beugré et Soro Élodie

title: I love my 4 kids and my 4 dogs, but sometimes I just need to shut the door on all of them
content:
My bedroom has become my escape, my sanctuary, my necessary respite from the hustle and bustle of a big family, including four kids and four rescue dogs.
When I'm in my room, and the door is closed, my family knows there are very few reasons why they would be allowed to disturb me.
Now, before you say, you chose this life, I want to acknowledge that I absolutely adore my family, including our little furry friends. However, like many families, our home can be noisy, busy, and at times, downright chaotic.
I deserve a break, and I refuse to feel bad about that.
My diagnosis changed me
I was never one to slip off to my room until I was diagnosed with breast cancer. Even as a type 1 diabetic, I would manage my highs and lows in the kitchen or living room, riding out the symptoms, no matter what was going on around me.
When breast cancer chose me, and I had a mastectomy, the six-week recovery meant that often, I would be laid up in my room, sipping water, napping, or watching a show. My chest incisions were fragile for weeks, and I still had young kids. I had to keep my surgical site protected.
This is when I broke my own "no TVs in the bedrooms" rule. My arms were useless during my recovery, so I couldn't hit up my usual go-to for entertainment, reading books. Instead, I binged multiple shows. At first, I hated being holed up in my room. I could hear my kids crying or laughing, and the dryer and dishwasher humming. Real life was happening out there, while I was stuck in my room.
My room stayed my retreat
As I recovered and stepped back into our hectic family life, I realized that my room was the only space that was just mine. My cozy (white) bedding, my completely sun-blocking curtains, minimal decor and clutter, and lamps that cast soft light across the room in the evenings when it was usually quiet — were all things that made me feel at peace. I learned that this was a space that my mind and body needed 8 years ago. Today, I still retreat to my room as often as I need.
Don't come knocking
My four kids, three of whom are teens now, know that if I am in my room with the door shut, the answer to any of their questions or requests is to go talk to their dad. I am unavailable, checked out, and relaxing.
As a mom and oldest daughter, I was conditioned to believe that I had to earn rest. To this day, I sometimes feel a wave of guilt for retreating to my room, taking a hot shower, and curling up in my bed with one of our rescues and a new book. The nagging voice in my head says that I should be doing something else, something more productive, something better, something expected. Yet I clap back to myself: Expected by whom?
I am trying to flip the script on the idea that I should be readily available and on guard at all times to meet the demands of my family and pets. Who decided that women are the default, the manager, the life coach, and the planner for the entire family, whether that be just one kiddo or multiple?
This is my simple indulgence
I have never been one to enjoy massages, pedicures, or one-day girls' trips. I don't think self-care isn't something that should be squeezed in once a quarter as a reward for white-knuckling motherhood. Instead, I have chosen a regular retreat to my own bedroom.
More on self care
Is this an escape? Sometimes, yes. When I'm overwhelmed, under the weather, or overstimulated from a full day of go-go-go, I need time to escape. I juggle so many roles, all of which demand a lot of my time and energy, and by acknowledging this, I choose to honor it by understanding and practicing the art of padding to my room, shutting the door, and letting out the sigh I've been holding in all day.
I am in my forties now, and I have unlearned so much that never served me or my family. I have embraced that a room retreat is modeling for my kids that, as they grow up, nurturing themselves and meeting their own needs is absolutely essential to staying mentally, physically, and emotionally healthy. It's one thing to tell them this, and I hope it's entirely more effective to regularly model it.

title: L’Boulevard 2026 names six winners of its Tremplin competition
content: After three days of live performances, two projects were selected in each category for their musical identity, artistic vision and ability to bring their work to life on stage.This year’s edition introduced a new approach: the winners were announced at the end of each competition night, allowing audiences to discover the projects selected by the juries without having to wait until the end of the event. The six winners came together again on Sunday, September 20, for the awards ceremony closing the 2026 edition of the L’Boulevard Tremplin.2026 winnersIn the Rap/Hip Hop category, the first prize went to Shinohidden from Berkane. After taking time to develop his identity, he began releasing his music in 2024. His rap moves between languages and tempos, with clear delivery over trap and atmospheric productions. With several tracks already online and collaborations with rapper Achflan, he has expanded into raï, blues, rock and gnaoua, citing Hoba Hoba Spirit among his influences. The result is a personal fusion rooted in lived experience.The second prize went to Casablanca’s BrownY Original, whose drill draws on the raw energy of trap, old-school rap and the discographies of artists such as 2Pac, Snoop Dogg, Dizzy Dros and Lil Baby. He gained attention with “3erfti Chno!!!” and “Lah Idir Chi Tawil ‘Ratatata’,” relying on direct lyrics and dark productions. After performing at L’Uzine and a showcase in Fez, he arrived at the Tremplin with a clearly defined sound, combining street aesthetics with stories drawn from everyday life.In the Fusion/Other Contemporary Music category, the first prize went to Metrotune from Casablanca-Settat. Formed in March 2026, the six-member band brings together a contemporary Moroccan fusion of salsa, rock and gnaoua. Its sound grew out of the different backgrounds of its members: rock- and metal-influenced guitar and bass, Latin piano, gnaoua percussion and chaâbi-inspired drums. The group initially focused on rearranging existing songs but is now working on original compositions and exploring new directions for Moroccan fusion music.The second prize went to Arinass from Fez, which explores Morocco’s rich musical traditions through more contemporary grooves. Blending gnaoua, aïta and chaâbi rhythms with reggae, rock and world music influences, the group builds its sound around vocals, traditional instruments and the energy of live performance. Its influences include Aziz Sahmaoui, Nass El Ghiwane, Tinariwen, Hoba Hoba Spirit, Alpha Blondy and Bob Marley.L’Boulevard 2026: Moroccan rap takes center stage at opening nightIn the Rock/Metal category, the first prize went to Lixivia from Salé. Formed in Salé in 2024, the band plays fast-paced crossover thrash, combining old-school thrash aggression with the urgency of hardcore punk, drawing inspiration from Municipal Waste, D.R.I. and Toxic Holocaust. Tight riffs, frantic tempos, mosh-pit energy and a contamination-themed aesthetic define Lixivia’s collision of metal and punk.The second prize went to Darih from Casablanca. Formed in the city in 2024, the band draws on the darker chapters of history, forgotten conflicts and North African esoteric folklore for its Black/Death Metal sound. Combining the precision of death metal with black metal atmospheres, its lyrics evoke the Moors, colonialism and local legends. The band cites Mgła, Bathory, Sepultura and Kreator among its influences. After performing at L’Uzine and on the First Stage at Tricinty Fest 2026, Darih already has several tracks to its name, including “1907” and “Liberation.”The Tremplin: a stage before a prizeSince 1999, the Tremplin has supported Morocco’s emerging music scene by giving artists access to a professional stage, an audience and industry attention. With this 24th edition, more than 765 Moroccan bands and artists will have performed on its stage since the competition was launched.Prize money was increased this year, with the first-place winners in each category receiving 15,000 dirhams and the second-place winners 10,000 dirhams.But the support does not end with the awards. From Monday, September 21 through September 26, the six winners will take part in a week-long training program at Boultek covering stage and vocal performance, recording, copyright, communication and digital distribution, musicians’ health and career development.Each of the six projects will also have the opportunity to record a track at Studio Hiba, a festival partner.

title: Relizane : un éboueur trouve un trésor… et le restitue intégralement
content:
En faisant sa tournée quotidienne dans les rues de Relizane, Abdelkader Mimouni dit Azzedine ne se doutait pas qu’il allait tomber, de bon matin, sur un petit trésor.
En mettant tout ce qui est plastique dans un sachet à part, cet éboueur, qui cumule 15 ans de service dans le service de collecte des déchets de cette ville de l’ouest algérien, remarque un sachet noir qui enveloppe une boîte soigneusement fermée. Il ne l’ouvre pas sur le champ.
A lire aussi : Inscription à la vaccination anti-Covid : prenez rendez-vous en ligne
A lire aussi : Algérie : révélations glaçantes sur le drame du bus de Oued El Harrach
« Nous sommes sortis comme d’habitude très tôt le matin, à 04h00, pour faire notre tournée. J’ai pris l’habitude de trier le plastique. Quand j’ai terminé, j’ai regardé ce que j’ai trié et j’ai retiré le sachet en question », raconte-t-il à Ennahar TV.
A lire aussi : Caricatures : de Chirac à Macron, comment la position de la France a évolué
Après la fin de sa tournée quotidienne, il rentre chez lui, et prend le sachet. Avec sa femme, il décide de l’ouvrir. Et puis, c’est la grande surprise. La boite est pleine de bijoux.
Relizane : un éboueur trouve une boîte pleine de bijoux
« Au début, en secouant la boîte, on pensait que c’était des jouets. Quand on l’a ouverte, nous avons trouvé de l’or. On a trouvé des noms, des numéros de téléphone », poursuit-il.
Sans réfléchir, et d’un commun accord avec sa femme, Azzedine referme la boite et appelle le bijoutier dont le numéro de téléphone se trouve sur un papier au milieu des bijoux. Le bijoutier reconnaît sa marchandise et prend contact avec la famille à qui il a vendu l’or d’une valeur de 3 millions de dinars.
« La famille qui a acheté les bijoux a reconnu la boîte », ajoute Azzedine. Pour le remercier, cette famille n’a pas manqué de lui offrir une somme d’argent dont le montant n’a pas été précisé. « J’étais endetté, et cette famille m’a aidé à payer les loyers en retard de la maison », conclut Azzedine.

title: What Cleveland’s Fight Reveals About Challenging Extractive Ownership
content:
Top Takeaways
After a corporate landlord in Cleveland let their buildings fall apart, tenants fought for habitable housing.
With the help of many partners, especially the city’s housing court, they eventually got the landlord’s lender to force a sale to a new owner.
However, by that time many tenants had been displaced, showing that new strategies are needed to hold landlords with an extractive short-term business model accountable more quickly.
Cleveland’s historic Shaker Square neighborhood contains a diverse array of housing types, including more than 80 apartment buildings. For decades, these apartments provided residents of varying incomes with quality housing in one of the country’s original transit-oriented districts. On the heels of the 2008 housing crisis, however, a silent predator crept into Shaker Square’s treasured rental housing stock.
These buildings were historically owned by respected local and regional family businesses or by established local and regional owner-operators. These owners nurtured the apartment market by valuing both tenants (as customers) and buildings (as long-term assets). Following the 2008 housing crisis, property values and interest rates were low. This combination made the buildings an attractive prospect for out-of-town buyers who saw opportunities for profit and began purchasing buildings in increasing numbers.
While the old-guard owners typically pursued a buy-and-hold strategy, new owners often did something very different—something more akin to a slash-and-burn approach. Their goals were to maximize short-term profit and sell off the property whenever profits started to dry up. Owners following this business model—logical from their perspective but disastrous for the buildings and tenants—have very little incentive to invest in even the most essential repairs, because their overriding interest is in maximizing revenue today, regardless of the longer-term consequences. We refer to the phenomenon of an owner prioritizing short-term profit at the expense of a building’s long-term viability as “extractive ownership.”
By 2015, most of the apartment buildings throughout Shaker Square were owned by out-of-town investors. By 2020, deferred maintenance was taking its toll, evidenced by a massive increase in major issues reported by tenants: no heat, out-of-order elevators, broken plumbing, etcetera.
Grassroots organizers and municipal building code enforcement entities waged a three-year battle against one unscrupulous investor engaged in this extractive practice. This sustained effort ultimately led to the successful transfer of three buildings to new ownership in 2025. Some of the tactics used and lessons learned may be instructive to others seeking successful models to push back against similarly extractive ownership elsewhere.
The SHAO Case: From Acquisition to Crisis
In January 2022, to great fanfare and media attention, Shaker Heights Apartments Owner LLC (SHAO) paid $12.4 million to acquire The Vista and The Residences, three eight-story multifamily apartment buildings totaling 250 units on the western edge of Shaker Square. Crain’s Cleveland Business identified the buyer as a joint venture between Chicago-based AMG Realty Group, whose investment strategy was to revitalize older, fading properties, and the Chetrit family, major players in New York real estate and the majority owners. “These are sophisticated and shrewd investors,” a broker with real estate firm Colliers told Crain’s. “These are not guys that overpay and not guys that don’t know what they’re doing. And they don’t lose money.” Occupancy was at 90 percent, although roughly 80 percent of the apartments needed upgrades at the time, according to Crain’s.
By October 2022, little rehabilitation had been completed, and management was poor and ever-changing. Tenants were fed up. Inconsistent heating and cooling, water and mold issues, electrical problems, and extensive structural damage continued to plague residents’ daily lives. Many elderly longtime tenants were forced to move, and those who remained endured the ongoing degradation of their units and common areas, including broken elevators for weeks on end. Broken garage and common doors allowed nonresidents to come and go at will, with squatters sleeping in the hallways. Vandalism and theft became common. Tenants sought the help of the Morelands Group, a local neighborhood organization that works to preserve, protect, and advocate for the historic apartment corridor of the Shaker Square community. With the Morelands Group’s assistance, tenants began a campaign to engage the owners, management, the media, policymakers, and the city of Cleveland about these conditions.
By December 2022, on-site management had all but disappeared, and emergency repairs ordered and paid for by the city were often necessary. “Everybody has a problem—just about everybody,” tenant leader Ron James told WKYC. In January 2023, almost exactly one year after SHAO bought the buildings, tenants began working with the Cleveland Housing Court, putting their rent in escrow to force crucial repairs. In February 2023, Cleveland Councilmember Deborah Gray traveled to New York to implore the owners to take care of their buildings, to no avail.
By April 2023, the city of Cleveland filed a public nuisance case against the owner, asking the court to declare the buildings a civil public nuisance and to place them in the hands of a receiver. The owners launched a well-resourced two-and-a-half-year defense in court, involving appeals to higher courts, discovery demands, stall tactics at the city’s Board of Building Standards and Appeals, and repeated requests for extensions.
Neglect Builds
During the time the case was pending, the buildings continued to deteriorate, and tenants’ distress continued to grow.
The housing department cited the owners for 302 interior and exterior violations. In one building, there were no working elevators for months. Tenants with mobility issues were trapped on upper floors, relying on friends and family to bring groceries and medications. During the winter, tenants had no heat for weeks at a time. The owners failed to repair damage caused by a fire from a space heater.
Mold and water damage continued to spread, and rat and insect infestations grew. A portion of the facade collapsed. The SHAO properties consistently ranked among the top 10 locations for police calls for service in Cleveland’s Fourth District.
Unsurprisingly, building occupancy fell from about 90 percent to about 40 percent.
Meanwhile, the owners were not paying their property taxes—the delinquent balance eventually exceeded $1.4 million—or their electricity bill, which accumulated a six-figure delinquent balance. The city had to intervene with the electric company to prevent it from shutting off all power to the building.
During that period, SHAO filed and prosecuted 63 eviction cases against tenants in these buildings. The Morelands Group provided paid counsel to more than 20 of these tenants.
A Breakthrough
In September 2025, as the public nuisance case continued to grind through the judicial process, Metropolitan Commercial Bank, the primary mortgage lender for the buildings, announced that a deal had been struck to have the buildings sold to Alba Construction of New York.It seems the lender had grown concerned enough about the state of the loan’s collateral to be willing to force a change in ownership.
Because Cleveland Housing Court had placed community control sanctions on the properties—including a prohibition of the “gifting, sale, or transfer” of the buildings without the court’s approval—the bank and SHAO had to pursue a settlement to obtain the court’s approval for a transfer.
The new owner pledged to remediate the buildings through a three-phase, multimillion-dollar rehabilitation. The city’s litigation costs and all other city expenses (more than $250,000) were reimbursed. Delinquent back taxes and all other outstanding liens were also paid at the time of transfer. Taken together, this means the taxpayer didn’t lose a single dime in the protracted effort to hold this extractive owner accountable, a result that other local governments facing similar problems can draw courage from.
Collaboration Made This Happen
The civic and housing infrastructure in Cleveland tends to be structurally siloed. Like the parable of the blind men and the elephant, this leads each stakeholder to see only part of the picture when a building is distressed. It takes intentional cross-jurisdictional efforts to overcome this and work effectively together to stabilize a distressed building, something that has not been the modus operandi in the past.
In the campaign against SHAO, the Morelands Group supported a different approach. We provided research capacity to piece together the facts and leveraged our institutional connections to coordinate a holistic push for civic and legal solutions to address the cascading issues of neglect.
The many players involved included:
- Tenants—organized by the Morelands Group—who were critical sources of on-the-ground information and drove the case forward. Their fortitude in continuing to document and report issues in the buildings, despite hostile ownership and difficult personal circumstances, provided the foundational evidence needed to bring the public nuisance case and to keep pressing for resolution.
- Council President Blaine Griffin and Councilmember Deborah Gray, whoprovided ongoing advocacy for the cause. Their commitment to their constituents and desire to address the core issue of an extractive owner provided the political cover for Cleveland’s Departments of Law and Building and Housing to bring the legal case, and their willingness to continue speaking about the issues kept the saga in the public eye until it was resolved.
- The city of Cleveland’s Building and Housing Department, which, under Director Sally Martin O’Toole, was instrumental in both assembling the case and pushing for prosecution.
- The city of Cleveland’s Department of Law, which, under the guidance of Law Director Mark Griffin, had to approve the overall legal approach and lend its time and expertise to push for prosecution. (Later, it would also be a key player in the settlement agreement.)
- Cleveland Housing Court, which used its powers to push for outcomes that affirmed the basic rights of tenants, as well as the right of the city to enforce basic habitability standards.
Lessons Learned
Current legal protections for tenants are ineffective when owners’ business models are extractive.
Most laws designed to protect tenants assume that owners are rational actors who want to maintain their buildings as rent-producing assets indefinitely. Extractive ownership models do not necessarily share this goal, and the resulting mismatch renders many legal strategies which tenants have historically used to assert their rights in court ineffective.
In this case, for example, the owners were willing to forgo rental revenue, allow tenants’ units to become uninhabitable, and incur substantial costs and even more substantial liabilities in order to continue operating extractively. Extractive owners don’t particularly fear the long-term consequences of such actions because their business models are oriented toward the short term. This meant that strategies such as rent-in-escrow, compel-to-repair orders, and fines resulting from code violations—all which were pursued by tenants in these buildings—were ineffective.
Pursuing damages in civil court is another possible avenue for tenant redress, which could, in theory, award damages large enough to matter to an extractive owner. The power imbalance between owner and tenant, however, makes it difficult to win in a timely fashion. This gap makes a broader strategy of pursuing justice via damages that can be scaled up both unlikely and impractical.
One determined tenant was so fed up with the conditions of her building that she filed a civil complaint in 2024 against the landlord for damages caused by mold, water infiltration, falling plaster, and more. She approached the Morelands Group in the spring of 2025 because the court magistrate had told her she needed an attorney. This tenant was facing what one tenant attorney calls the “justice gap.” Her income exceeded the Legal Aid criteria for assistance, but even a discounted attorney’s fee was financially out of reach. In this case, the Morelands Group bridged that funding gap. Finally, in June 2026, the tenant received a favorable judgment for $15,000—but a judgment simply gives the tenant the right to collect. Since SHAO is now a semi-defunct LLC without assets and its controlling interests are in New York, the tenant has been unable to collect the money as of this writing.
The judicial process may have saved the building, but it moved too slowly to prevent the displacement of tenants.
The owner successfully dragged the case on for so long with delay and appeal tactics—while letting the building decay—that the majority of long-term tenants who wanted to stay were ultimately “evicted through neglect.” These tenants relocated because the conditions in their units became a threat to their health they could tolerate no longer.
This is not a criticism of the judicial process per se—due process and property rights are ingrained in the judicial process for good reason. However, these delays had an immense impact on the day-to-day lives of the tenants, because while the delays were occurring, tenants still had to deal with the deteriorating situation on the ground. We observed, for example, a one-month delay in a case hearing to accommodate an attorney’s personal schedule. For tenants in one building, that meant an additional month without a working elevator, trapping seniors with mobility issues in upper-floor units. As one tenant on an upper floor said during the time, “I’m a hostage in my own apartment—and I’m paying for it.”
From our perspective, judicial delay happened in two main places. First, as discussed, there are situations in which the judge has discretion to set the “next date” for an element of the case. We urge the courts to move cases forward as efficiently as reasonably possible in situations like this, where residents’ lives are being substantially affected.
Second, the appeals process: This is a fundamental part of due process, and we understand the high caseload that appellate courts face. However, extractive owners are aware of the delays in obtaining appellate rulings and regularly employ appeals to intentionally stall local cases for months, if not years. SHAO’s appeal to the Ohio’s Eighth District Court of Appeals led to almost a year during which progress through the judicial system ceased entirely, even as building conditions continued to worsen.
A focused media strategy helped marshal support for a solution.
Throughout this struggle, the local media helped amplify the voices of the tenants and the neighborhood. TV segments showing the disrepair in the buildings and articles in local media outlets were extremely useful in galvanizing awareness of and support for a solution.
Research and data are critical elements of success.
Cleveland, like many municipalities, has a research gap in its civic and housing infrastructure. Much of the information needed to build and advance a case like this one is in the public record. However, data is spread across multiple databases and presented in difficult-to-navigate, jargon-filled formats. Most city- and county-level departments lack the capacity to focus on detailed neighborhood-level strategies, and the bandwidth to connect the dots at the individual owner level.
To bridge this gap for the Shaker Square neighborhood, the Morelands Group created its own research infrastructure. Spreadsheets and maps maintained by the group combine hyperlocal information gathered from tenants and neighbors, along with available public data. Once data is collected in this holistic, usable format, it can be used for strategic planning and to communicate to partners what the neighborhood is seeing on the ground.
Cleveland Housing Court’s do-not-sell order gave local interests leverage.
Having a do-not-sell order imposed by the housing court as part of its community control sanctions turned out to be critically important. This forced the lender to come to the table with local partners, craft a settlement deal with the plaintiff (the city of Cleveland), and have that settlement approved by Cleveland Housing Court.
The city’s Residents Firstlegislation would have helped maintain housing standards.
Although not yet enacted when this case began, Cleveland’s recently passed Residents First legislation adds key tools that could have helped hold the owner accountable. Key provisions of this legislation would have helped us on the ground:
– A Local Agent In Charge: A designated person who lives locally and is legally responsible for the building would have given tenants—and the courts—more direct access to an accountable individual.
– Rental registration requirements could have been used to compel repairs earlier in the process, especially after serious health and safety concerns were documented.
Civil nuisance litigation appears to be one of the most viable tools for stabilizing buildings—but it has weaknesses.
While civil nuisance litigation is extremely useful as a means to compel owners to keep buildings up to code, neither of the two backstop mechanisms for when the owner is actively noncompliant worked effectively in this case.
1. Community control sanctions imposed by Cleveland Housing Court
The owner was able to neutralize or at least indefinitely postpone most of the consequences of the community control order by appealing it. A stay was granted on almost all the community control stipulations while the appeal was pending. (One notable exception was the do-not-sell order.)
2. Appointment of a receiver to take day-to-day control and stabilize the property
This was what the city’s prosecution team ultimately pushed for in the case against SHAO. Ohio receivership law is structured so the receiver is responsible for paying the upfront costs to stabilize the buildings; the expectation is that they can rely on rental revenue from existing tenants to do so. However, in cases like this, where upfront costs are high due to neglect and rent revenue is limited by an initially high level of vacancy, a receiver would almost certainly have needed to invest their own capital, or at least take out a loan, to finance the upfront repairs. In a relatively weak housing market such as Cleveland’s, this can involve substantial risk. The repairs may cost more than the building is ultimately worth when there are large amounts of deferred maintenance. We are not aware of an entity that would have applied to serve as receiver of the SHAO buildings had the legal case not been drawn to an early conclusion by the intervention of the lender.
It was the lender who ultimately forced an ownership transfer.
In the end, it was the lender—not the owner—who acted. Local advocacy, political pressure, and legal action all made the situation untenable for SHAO, and we believe the courts likely would have eventually ruled in favor of the city’s prosecution. Ultimately, however, it was the lender’s financial leverage that ended the stalemate, producing a faster resolution than the judicial process alone could have achieved.
This suggests a potential opportunity for future cases. Access to data on liens and loan payments could provide early warnings of fiscal distress. Outreach to lenders earlier in the process—arming them with clear local evidence of harm—may be a viable strategy to pursue. A speedier conclusion would have minimized harm to tenants and the buildings and, presumably, would have been in the lender’s best interest.
The SHAO case illustrates both the fragility and the potential of Cleveland’s housing ecosystem. It shows that when tenants, community organizers, city officials, and courts align around a shared goal, even deeply distressed properties can be rescued. Yet it also exposed systemic weaknesses—slow judicial timelines, opaque ownership structures, and limited coordination—that allow extractive ownership to persist far too long and cause lasting harm to buildings and tenants.
The challenge now is to move this work upstream. Cleveland needs to increase its capacity to recognize the warning signs of extractive ownership earlier, connect the dots across properties and public systems, and bring the right partners together before a building reaches crisis. The experience with SHAO suggests that this is possible, and that doing so could protect not only individual buildings and tenants, but entire neighborhoods from the cycle of disinvestment and displacement.
Adapted from ‘Everybody Has a Problem’: A Case Study in Combating Extractive Ownership, released by the Morelands Group, Cleveland, Ohio, November 2025. Meg Weingart, Convener.

title: Clinical usefulness of objective tongue image devices monitoring in temporal tongue color: a demonstration of successively treated cases with traditional medicines
content: BackgroundIn Kampo medicine (traditional Japanese medicine), the diagnostic method of observing a patient's tongue is called the ‘tongue diagnosis’. Information provided by observation of a patient's tongue is used to help select prescriptions at the initial consultation, monitor treatment effectiveness after therapy begins, and determine whether prescriptions should be changed. Kampo practitioners must therefore accurately compare the patient's past tongue condition with the current condition. However, it can be difficult to remember the precise details regarding a patient's previous tongue's appearance and to consistently make accurate comparisons. Given the need for objective and reproducible method of documenting tongue findings, we investigated the usefulness of our developed Tongue Image Analyzing System (TIAS). The application of the TIAS for two representative patients is described herein.MethodsWe retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent tongue photography after providing informed consent and selected two cases with contrasting degrees of longitudinal changes in tongue findings. One patient demonstrated subtle changes in tongue color that were difficult to detect with the naked eye, and the other patient showed marked tongue color changes accompanied by changes in the heterogeneity of the tongue coating. We obtained the tongue color values in each case from tongue images photographed by TIAS as RGB data and converted into the CIE L*a*b* color space.ResultsThe tongue color of case1 was analyzed at three time points. The color difference from the first consultation (calculated as ΔE00 using L*a*b* values) increased by ΔE00 1–2 after 42 days. This change was too subtle to be perceived by the naked eye. The tongue color of case 2, tongue color was analyzed at five time points. The color difference between the first consultation and 105 days later was ΔE00 10.08, indicating a substantial change in tongue color.ConclusionTIAS enables standardized longitudinal tongue imaging and facilitates the objective and quantitative comparison of subtle changes in tongue color that may be difficult to discern visually. These findings suggest that TIAS may be useful for objectively documenting and comparing longitudinal changes in tongue findings in clinical practice.

title: Wenn Antwort kommt - Wie lange die Wiener auf einen Arzttermin warten
content:
Monatelang auf einen Kassen-Facharzt warten – für viele Patienten ist das längst Realität. Doch ausgerechnet Wien schneidet im Bundesländer-Vergleich deutlich besser ab. Eine neue Studie zeigt, wo es besonders schnell geht – und in welchem Fach selbst Wiener zwei Monate warten.
Drei Tage bis zum Radiologen, 64 bis zum Psychiater: Wer in Wien einen Kassenarzt sucht, erlebt je nach Fach enorme Unterschiede. Trotzdem haben es Wiener im Bundesländer-Vergleich noch am besten erwischt. Das zeigt die Wartezeitenstudie der Plattform krankenversichern.at. Der Median über 13 Facharztrichtungen liegt in Wien bei 22 Tagen – österreichweit sind es 34 Tage.
Teils mehrere Wochen Unterschied
Wie groß die Unterschiede innerhalb der Stadt sind, zeigt der Blick auf die einzelnen Fächer. In der Psychiatrie beträgt die Wartezeit im Median 64 Tage, in der Inneren Medizin 42, in der Neurologie 35 und in der Kardiologie 34 Tage. Deutlich schneller geht es bei Radiologie mit drei Tagen, Orthopädie mit fünf und HNO mit sechs Tagen. Beim Hausarzt liegt die durchschnittliche Wartezeit bei einem Tag.
Nur der erste Termin
Für Wien wurden 315 Facharzt-Anfragen ausgewertet. Angefragt wurden nicht akute Routine- und Vorsorgetermine. Gewertet wurde jeweils der erste jeweils von der Ordination angebotene Termin.
Manche Ordinationen nehmen niemanden auf
Die Zahlen zeigen allerdings nur jene Ordinationen, die überhaupt einen Termin angeboten haben. Aufnahmestopps und Ordinationen ohne Rückmeldung sind nicht enthalten. Der Aufwand, zunächst überhaupt einen aufnehmenden Kassenarzt zu finden, wird damit nicht abgebildet.
Man zahlt mit Lebenszeit
Was das bedeutet, kann jeder Wiener am eigenen Leib erleben. Studienleiter Sebastian Arthofer bringt es auf den Punkt: „Der Kassenarzt kostet dem Patienten kein Geld, er hat einen Wartepreis. Bezahlt wird er in Wochen. Wer die nicht hat, bezahlt den Termin im Wahlarztbereich in Euro – selbst oder finanziert über eine private Krankenversicherung.“

title: Houston now requires air conditioning in all rentals, making cooling a housing standard
content:
In one of Texas' hottest major cities, air conditioning is no longer an optional perk for renters.
Houston City Council voted to require landlords to provide cooling in every rental unit, making AC a basic housing standard.
Here's what to know
Landlords now have 120 days — until December — to equip every rental unit with some form of cooling, according to the Houston Chronicle, whether it be central air, a window AC, or a portable unit.
Council approved the ordinance 12-2, ending Houston's longstanding "window screen exemption." Under that rule, owners could satisfy housing-code standards with screened windows and doors instead of refrigerated air.
In a city where intense summer heat can threaten people's health, that exception became increasingly notable. Going forward, a unit without AC will be handled through the normal code-enforcement system where residents can file a complaint, the health department can inspect the property, and landlords who do not fix the issue can face citations or end up in municipal court.
Backers of the change say it puts Houston in line with other big Texas cities and recognizes cooling as part of a safe, livable home rather than a luxury amenity.
More background
The change comes after several years of record summer heat, coinciding with an increase in heat-related deaths in the Houston area. Indoor cooling can make a major difference for older adults, children, and people with health conditions that get worse in extreme heat.
A 2023 survey put the number of rental households without air conditioning across the Houston metro at 20,400. But that estimate includes homes outside Houston city limits, so not all of those units would be covered by the ordinance.
The Houston fight is also part of a broader Texas debate. State lawmakers tried to create a statewide requirement for air conditioning in rentals, but that effort stalled amid objections to adding more regulations for property owners.
Some Houston officials expressed similar worries. Mayor John Whitmire said he was "fearful" the rule could increase rents and utility bills, while Council Member Twila Carter said, "My concern is for the people that this policy is intended to protect. This comes at a heavy cost, and it will put people on the streets."
What's being done?
Amy Peck, a council member and realtor, said Houston already requires heat even though it had never required air conditioning. She also said renters often had little recourse when an existing AC unit broke and was not repaired.
The ordinance was backed not just by housing advocates but also by the Houston Apartment Association, and there was no apparent landlord opposition during public hearings.
Julia Orduña of Texas Housers explained, "It comes down to that right to choose how much you're going to pay for electricity. It's not about living with or without AC in your unit, it's about deciding when to turn the AC on and off."
Council Member Alejandra Salinas said, "All Houstonians deserve a right to rest from heat, and that's what this ordinance is going to do."

title: New Brunswick, Canada, wins North America's tap water crown after 33-city taste test
content:
Winning an award for tap water may not sound glamorous, but it says a lot about a system people rely on every day. Fredericton, New Brunswick, has now earned that distinction, taking the title of North America's best-tasting tap water.
Here's what to know
Taste, aroma, and consistency were the measures used in the American Water Works Association competition highlighted by Toronto Culture. The outlet said Fredericton finished first ahead of 32 other regional winners.
Each day, roughly 5.3 million gallons (20 million liters) pass through Fredericton's water network.
Part of the water's taste comes from the mineral content in groundwater drawn from an aquifer beneath downtown Fredericton. The system relies on 11 wells connected to that source.
To keep the supply within Canadian drinking water guidelines, the city collects samples each week from about 50 sites.
More background
Reliable municipal water can have benefits beyond taste. When residents trust the quality of their tap water, they may be less likely to buy bottled alternatives, saving money while reducing single-use plastic waste.
Fredericton's water comes from an aquifer. As groundwater passes through natural layers of earth, it can be filtered before reaching treatment and distribution systems.
Weekly testing helps support that resource with consistent oversight.
What's being done?
Water quality can shift across a distribution system. Testing helps officials confirm that the water reaching homes and businesses remains safe and consistent, not just at the source.
Protecting groundwater sources, investing in treatment and delivery systems, and maintaining frequent testing can help produce consistent results.
Where can I learn more?
These stories take a closer look at the challenges surrounding tap water quality, safety, and supply. They cover PFAS concerns in U.S. drinking water, health risks linked to contamination, and California systems turning wastewater into freshwater.
• Across the U.S., new national maps reveal widespread PFAS concerns in household tap water.
• Researchers found the health impact of contaminated U.S. tap water may be severe.
• In Pennsylvania, residents demanded answers after bad chemicals in our water raised alarm.
• In California, a treatment plant shows treated sewage can become freshwater again.

title: Inspired by Grandparents, Designer Creates Canes For Elderly That Send SOS, Monitor BP
content:
Shreya Thakkar watched her grandparents age in Vadodara. “Watching my mother serve as their caretaker taught me the importance of compassion and empathy in the care of the elderly,” she recalls.
That experience stayed with her. In Los Angeles, she volunteered at senior living facilities, hearing stories that strengthened her interest in assistive technology and ageing.
“At senior living facilities in Los Angeles, I was able to hear their stories and truly experience their lives, further solidifying my passion for assistive technology,” she says.
Her research changed how she saw ageing. “When older adults were asked about their dreams, a majority of them mentioned independence and the joy of meandering,” she says. Their need was not only for support.
She found that ageing products missed this need. “We must overcome the myth that ageing equates to feebleness and passivity,” she says, questioning stereotypes around growing older.
Her answer was ‘Wander On’, a smart cane and walker designed to offer support without taking away independence. The cane combines mobility assistance with safety, health monitoring, and GPS tracking.
The Wander On Assist 01 has an adjustable height, built-in pedometer, and ergonomic design. It can track blood pressure, temperature, and pulse, while an SOS button sends an emergency signal.
But getting there was not easy. “Every time my design failed, I gained invaluable insights that allowed me to tweak and improve,” Shreya says. Feedback helped her understand the project’s pain points.
She also designed the Wander On Assist 02 walker, with wheels, a seat, GPS, smart home connectivity, and hand gesture detection. Users can sit or stand, check health details, and share them with contacts.
The idea was bigger than a device. “It strengthens the independence equilibrium that one always strives to preserve,” she explains. She wanted seniors to age in place with dignity, independence, and grace.
Her aim remains clear: “It’s my goal to help older people achieve greater levels of autonomy, independence, mobility, and connection through my work.” She sees this as only the beginning.
